result:
Lichen is the thing I'd choose to be amazed by, if amazement were rationed.

It looks like nothing: a crust of gray-green paint on a gravestone, a smear of orange on a seaside rock. But a lichen is not one organism. It's a fungus and an alga, sometimes with a yeast along for the ride, living so tightly together that for centuries naturalists took them for a single plant. The fungus builds the house; the alga makes the food. Neither looks anything like the lichen when grown alone. Together they produce a body that neither partner holds the blueprint for.

And they are patient. Some map lichens in the Arctic grow less than a millimeter a year and may be thousands of years old. Geologists use them as clocks: measure the width of a patch on a moraine and you can estimate when the glacier retreated. A stain on a rock, quietly keeping time.

They are tough, too. Lichens have survived eighteen months on the outside of the space station, in vacuum and raw sunlight, and resumed photosynthesizing back home. Yet they're delicate about air: they vanished from coal-era cities and crept back as the skies cleared.

What I like most is how lichen unsettles the idea of the individual. We want our categories clean: one creature here, another there. Lichen is a relationship that grew a body. Next time you pass an old stone wall, look closely. That gray smudge is a partnership, a clock, and a survivor at once.
